monochromatic-color-generator.quickAnswer: A monochromatic palette keeps one hue and varies only lightness. From #4A90D9 (HSL 211, 65%, 57%), the tool spreads shades evenly: at 30% lightness the math gives #1B4B7E, at 70% it gives #81B1E4. Because the hue never changes, every shade sits naturally beside the others - the safest palette a designer can pick.
keyFacts: Monochromatic = one hue, one saturation, many lightness levels.
The tool spreads shades evenly between 12% and 88% lightness so nothing is pure black or white.
Same-hue palettes can never clash - they are the safest choice for beginners.
Use the darkest shade for text, mid shades for UI elements, lightest for backgrounds.
Monochromatic schemes work beautifully for data charts where one series needs emphasis levels.
howTo: Enter your base color with the picker or a HEX code like #4A90D9.
Choose how many shades you want: 4, 6 or 8.
Shades appear instantly, evenly spread from dark to light.
Tap any shade to copy its HEX code.
Use dark shades for text and light shades for backgrounds in your design.
monochromatic-color-generator.formula:
Each shade = HSL(base hue, base saturation, L), with L spread evenly from 12% to 88%.
Example: #4A90D9 -> HSL(211, 65%, 57%).
At L = 30%: HSL(211, 65%, 30%) = RGB(27, 75, 126) = #1B4B7E.
At L = 70%: HSL(211, 65%, 70%) = RGB(129, 177, 228) = #81B1E4.
monochromatic-color-generator.workedExample:
Base #4A90D9, converted to HSL(211, 65%, 57%):
1. Keep hue 211 and saturation 65% fixed.
2. At 30% lightness: chroma math gives RGB(27, 75, 126), which is #1B4B7E - a deep navy.
3. At 70% lightness: the same math gives RGB(129, 177, 228), which is #81B1E4 - a soft sky blue.
4. With 6 shades, lightness steps are 12, 27, 42, 58, 73 and 88 - a smooth ramp with no jumps.
benefits: Impossible to clash - one hue always looks intentional and calm.
Perfect for monochrome brand identities and minimalist interfaces.
Great for charts: darker = more important, lighter = less important.
Copy any shade with one tap - no design tool needed.
limitations: One hue can feel flat; most designs add one accent color for energy.
Adjacent mid shades may be hard to tell apart - check contrast for text use.
Very dark shades on black backgrounds can disappear; test in context.

faqs.q: What does monochromatic mean in color theory?
faqs.a: It means a palette built from a single hue. You vary only lightness (and sometimes saturation) to create depth, so the palette is automatically harmonious.

faqs.q: Why does the tool stop at 12% and 88% lightness?
faqs.a: Pure black and pure white add no hue information and are rarely useful as palette shades. Stopping just short keeps every shade recognizably part of the family.

faqs.q: Can I use this for a dark-mode palette?
faqs.a: Yes - use the darkest 2-3 shades as your dark-mode surfaces and text, and the lightest shades for highlights.

faqs.q: How is this different from tints and shades?
faqs.a: Tints mix with white and shades mix with black in RGB space. This tool moves lightness in HSL space, which preserves the perceived color family more smoothly.

faqs.q: How many shades should I pick?
faqs.a: Four is enough for a simple UI (text, primary, border, background). Six to eight suits design systems that need hover, disabled and divider states.

faqs.q: Will these shades pass accessibility contrast checks?
faqs.a: Dark shades on light shades usually pass easily, but mid-on-mid pairs can fail. Always run the specific pair through a contrast checker before shipping text.

labels.invalidHex: That HEX code is not valid. Use 3 or 6 hex digits, like #4A9 or #4A90D9.
